4|Abiraterone plus prednisone added to androgen deprivation
5|therapy and docetaxel in de novo metastatic castration-
6|sensitive prostate cancer (PEACE-1): a multicentre, open-
7|label, randomised, phase 3 study with a 2 × 2 factorial design
8|Karim Fizazi, Stéphanie Foulon, Joan Carles, Guilhem Roubaud, Ray McDermott, Aude Fléchon, Bertrand Tombal, Stéphane Supiot,
9|Dominik Berthold, Philippe Ronchin, Gabriel Kacso, Gwenaëlle Gravis, Fabio Calabro, Jean-François Berdah, Ali Hasbini, Marlon Silva,
10|Antoine Thiery-Vuillemin, Igor Latorzeff, Loïc Mourey, Brigitte Laguerre, Sophie Abadie-Lacourtoisie, Etienne Martin, Claude El Kouri,
11|Anne Escande, Alvar Rosello, Nicolas Magne, Friederike Schlurmann, Frank Priou, Marie-Eve Chand-Fouche, Salvador Villà Freixa,
12|Muhammad Jamaluddin, Isabelle Rieger, Alberto Bossi, on behalf of the PEACE-1 investigators*
13|Summary
14|Background Current standard of care for metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer supplements androgen
15|deprivation therapy with either docetaxel, second-generation hormonal therapy, or radiotherapy. We aimed to
16|evaluate the efficacy and safety of abiraterone plus prednisone, with or without radiotherapy, in addition to
17|standard of care.
18|Methods We conducted an open-label, randomised, phase 3 study with a 2 × 2 factorial design (PEACE-1) at
19|77 hospitals across Belgium, France, Ireland, Italy, Romania, Spain, and Switzerland. Eligible patients were male,
20|aged 18 years or older, with histologically confirmed or cytologically confirmed de novo metastatic prostate
21|adenocarcinoma, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0-1 (or 2 due to bone pain).
22|Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) to standard of care (androgen deprivation therapy alone or with
23|intravenous docetaxel 75 mg/m2 once every 3 weeks), standard of care plus radiotherapy, standard of care plus
24|abiraterone (oral 1000 mg abiraterone once daily plus oral 5 mg prednisone twice daily), or standard of care plus
25|radiotherapy plus abiraterone. Neither the investigators nor the patients were masked to treatment allocation. The
26|coprimary endpoints were radiographic progression-free survival and overall survival. Abiraterone efficacy was
27|first assessed in the overall population and then in the population who received androgen deprivation therapy
28|with docetaxel as standard of care (population of interest). This study is ongoing and is registered with
29|ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT01957436.
30|Findings Between Nov 27, 2013, and Dec 20, 2018, 1173 patients were enrolled (one patient subsequently withdrew
31|consent for analysis of his data) and assigned to receive standard of care (n=296), standard of care plus radiotherapy
32|(n=293), standard of care plus abiraterone (n=292), or standard of care plus radiotherapy plus abiraterone (n=291).
33|Median follow-up was 3·5 years (IQR 2·8-4·6) for radiographic progression-free survival and 4·4 years (3·5-5·4)
34|for overall survival. Adjusted Cox regression modelling revealed no interaction between abiraterone and
35|radiotherapy, enabling the pooled analysis of abiraterone efficacy. In the overall population, patients assigned to
36|receive abiraterone (n=583) had longer radiographic progression-free survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0·54, 99·9% CI
37|0·41-0·71; p<0·0001) and overall survival (0·82, 95·1% CI 0·69-0·98; p=0·030) than patients who did not receive
38|abiraterone (n=589). In the androgen deprivation therapy with docetaxel population (n=355 in both with
39|abiraterone and without abiraterone groups), the HRs were consistent (radiographic progression-free survival 0·50,
40|99·9% CI 0·34-0·71; p<0·0001; overall survival 0·75, 95·1% CI 0·59-0·95; p=0·017). In the androgen deprivation
41|therapy with docetaxel population, grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 217 (63%) of 347 patients who
42|received abiraterone and 181 (52%) of 350 who did not; hypertension had the largest difference in occurrence
43|(76 [22%] patients and 45 [13%], respectively). Addition of abiraterone to androgen deprivation therapy plus
44|docetaxel did not increase the rates of neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, fatigue, or neuropathy compared with
45|androgen deprivation therapy plus docetaxel alone.
46|Interpretation Combining androgen deprivation therapy, docetaxel, and abiraterone in de novo metastatic castration-
47|sensitive prostate cancer improved overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival with a modest increase
48|in toxicity, mostly hypertension. This triplet therapy could become a standard of care for these patients.

62|Introduction
63|After several decades with no substantial progress, the
64|treatment of de novo (synchronous) metastatic prostate
65|cancer has drastically evolved in the past 10 years
66|with the addition of diverse treatments to androgen
67|deprivation therapy (ADT), the former standard of care
68|(SOC). The prognosis for men with de novo metastatic
69|castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) has been
70|improved by using ADT concomitantly with either
71|docetaxel1-5 or one of the second-generation androgen
72|receptor axis inhibitors (abiraterone,6-8 apalutamide,9 or
73|enzalutamide10,11). In 2018, radiotherapy to the primary
74|tumour was also shown to extend the overall survival of
75|patients with low-volume metastatic burden.12 The
76|benefits of these various combinatory therapies were
77|confirmed by meta-analyses13-15 and have helped to shape
78|the current guidelines for the treatment of mCSPC.16-18
79|Nevertheless, it remains to be established whether
80|merging some of these new therapies could provide
81|further clinical benefits and, if so, what combination
82|might be most suitable for de novo mCSPC.19 Conducted
83|by a European consortium (PEACE),20 this study aimed to
84|evaluate the efficacy and safety of abiraterone plus
85|prednisone, with or without radiotherapy, in addition to
86|SOC (ADT with or without docetaxel).
87|Methods
88|Study design and participants
89|We conducted an open-label, randomised, active-
90|controlled, phase 3 study with a 2 × 2 factorial design
91|(PEACE-1) at 77 sites across seven European countries
92|(Belgium, France, Ireland, Italy, Romania, Spain, and
93|Switzerland). The complete list of inclusion and exclusion
94|criteria is provided in the appendix (pp 5-6). Briefly, male
95|patients aged 18 years or older with histologically confirmed
96|or cytologically confirmed prostate adenocarcinoma
97|documented as de novo metastatic by bone scan, CT, or
98|MRI (according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid
99|Tumors [RECIST] version 1.1 criteria) and an Eastern
100|Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status
101|of 0-1 (or 2 due to bone pain) were eligible for inclusion,
102|provided they had received ADT for no more than
103|3 months before randomisation and had at least 6 weeks
104|between the initiation of ADT and the first docetaxel
105|dose. Patients with a pure small-cell carcinoma, or
106|previous prostate cancer treated by a definitive local
107|treatment were not eligible. All participants provided
108|written informed consent before any study-specific
109|procedures or randomisation were initiated.
110|The initial protocol was reviewed and first approved on
111|July 10, 2013, by the French Independent Ethics
112|Committee (Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile de
113|France VII). The protocol complied with the ethical
114|principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was
115|approved by Institutional Review Boards at each study
116|site. The trial conformed with the International
117|Conference on Harmonization and Good Clinical
118|Practice guidelines, and applicable regulatory require
119|ments. Steering and Independent Data Monitoring
120|Committees roles and members are described in the
121|appendix (pp 3-4).
122|Two major protocol amendments were made during
123|the accrual period, to account for the evolution of SOC
124|for men with mCSPC. Although ADT alone was the SOC
125|when the trial began recruitment in 2013, the protocol
126|was amended on Oct 5, 2015 (273 patients had already
127|been accrued), to allow for docetaxel use in SOC
128|worldwide, after ADT with docetaxel had shown
129|improvement in overall survival.2,3 Then, in 2017, ADT
130|plus abiraterone was also shown to improve overall
131|Research in context
132|Evidence before this study
133|We searched PubMed from Jan 1, 1984, to Dec 31, 2012, for
134|papers in English, using the terms "prostate cancer",
135|"metastases", and "phase 3 trial", and found 16 studies. When
136|the PEACE-1 trial began in 2013, androgen deprivation
137|therapy (ADT) had for several decades been the standard of
138|care for men with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate
139|cancer (mCSPC). All randomised trials conducted before the
140|mid-2010s had not shown improvement in outcomes with
141|new therapies compared with ADT. During recruitment for the
142|PEACE-1 trial (2013-18), overall survival of patients with de
143|novo mCSPC was shown to be improved by combining ADT
144|with either docetaxel or one of the second-generation
145|androgen receptor axis inhibitors (abiraterone, apalutamide,
146|or enzalutamide) and radiotherapy to the primary tumour, in
147|men with low metastatic burden. It had not yet been shown
148|whether combining some of these new therapies with ADT in
149|triple therapy could provide further clinical benefits.
150|Added value of this study
151|To our knowledge, PEACE-1 is the first trial to show that
152|a triple systemic therapy-consisting of ADT, docetaxel,
153|and a second-generation androgen signalling inhibitor
154|(abiraterone, combined with prednisone)-improves both
155|radiographic progression-free survival and overall survival in
156|patients with de novo mCSPC, without excessively increasing
157|toxicity (mostly hypertension and aminotransferase increase).
158|Implications of all the available evidence
159|The findings from the PEACE-1 trial, combined with the evidence
160|from other studies, add weight to the concept that systemic
161|treatment intensification provides clinical benefit for men with
162|mCSPC and illustrate that early treatment intensification is more
163|effective than identical or similar treatments being used
164|sequentially when the disease has become castration-resistant.
165|At a minimum, patients with mCSPC with a high metastatic
166|burden who are fit enough to be treated with docetaxel should
167|be considered for this triple systemic therapy.

16|Randomisation and masking
17|Eligible patients were centrally randomly assigned in the
18|Alea Clinical Portal), in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, to SOC, SOC plus
19|radiotherapy, SOC plus abiraterone (abiraterone plus
20|prednisone), or SOC plus radiotherapy plus abiraterone.
21|This randomisation process was performed via the
22|Tenalea autonomous software, solely accessed by the trial
23|data manager within the Epidemioloy and Biostatistics
24|facility of the Gustave Roussy Center in Villejuif, France
25|until 2015, then by each investigator.
26|Randomisation was done using a minimisation
27|algorithm, stratified by study site, ECOG performance
28|status (0 vs 1-2), type of ADT (gonadotropin-releasing
29|hormone agonist vs antagonist vs bilateral orchiectomy),
30|planned administration of docetaxel (yes vs no), and
31|disease extent or burden based on metastatic status
32|(lymph node metastases only vs bone metastases [with or
33|without lymph node metastases] vs visceral metastases).
34|A similar weight was given to each of the five
35|stratification factors, with 80% probability to minimise
36|imbalance in the number of patients assigned to each
37|treatment group. As the case report form gathered
38|information for patient stratification according to
39|high-volume versus low-volume metastatic burden
40|classification (as defined in the CHAARTED study2 [high
41|volume was defined as the presence of visceral
42|metastases or at least four bone lesions with one beyond
43|the vertebral bodies and pelvis]), this later classification
44|was retained to enable inter-trial comparisons. No
45|masking was performed in this study.
46|Procedures
47|In all patients in the study, ADT was planned to be
48|continuously maintained by either a gonadotropin-
49|releasing hormone agonist or antagonist, or bilateral
50|orchiectomy. Patients assigned to receive docetaxel as part
51|of SOC with continuous ADT were to receive six cycles of
52|intravenous docetaxel (75 mg/m2 per cycle; maximum
53|dose of 150 mg per cycle), to be administered every
54|3 weeks (plus or minus 3 days). Granulocyte colony-
55|stimulating factor (G-CSF) injections after each docetaxel
56|cycle were recommended until the protocol amendment
57|on Jan 22, 2018, made G-CSF prophylaxis mandatory for
58|patients who received docetaxel. The first docetaxel cycle
59|had to be administered within 14 days after randomisation
60|and be at least 6 weeks after ADT initiation. Patients
61|assigned to receive abiraterone received 1000 mg of
62|abiraterone (four 250 mg tablets, orally) once daily plus
63|prednisone 5 mg orally twice daily, starting within 6 weeks
64|after ADT initiation. PEACE-1 began accrual in 2013,
65|before the LATITUDE6 and the STAMPEDE7 abiraterone
66|trials were reported and before abiraterone was approved
67|for mCSPC, which is why we used 10 mg of prednisone,
68|similar to what is approved for metastatic castration-
69|resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Abiraterone and
70|prednisone (hereafter referred to as abiraterone) were
71|administered until disease progression to castration
72|resistance, withdrawal of consent, unacceptable toxicity,
73|or death. Patients assigned to receive radiotherapy
74|(74 Gy in 37 fractions administered over 7-8 weeks)
75|were planned to start radiotherapy at least 3 weeks
76|after docetaxel completion (but no more than 8 weeks
77|after completion). Treatments given after disease
78|progression followed common practice, and investigators
79|were able to change therapy as they thought was most
80|appropriate, on the basis of prostate-specific antigen
81|(PSA) concentration variation or clinical progression,
82|even in absence of radiographical evidence. The treatment
83|flow chart is depicted in the appendix (p 10).
84|Every enrolled patient was to be followed-up for a
85|duration of 10 years. The complete list of assessments
86|performed at each visit and follow-up intervals are
87|detailed in the appendix (pp 12-13). Survival status data
88|were gathered within 3 months of the cutoff date for
89|97% of patients.
90|Outcomes
91|The coprimary endpoints were radiographic progression-
92|free survival and overall survival. Radiographical pro
93|gression of soft-tissue lesions was evaluated by either CT
94|or MRI, on the basis of RECIST version 1.1. Progression
95|of bone lesions was assessed by bone scan according to
96|the adapted version of Prostate Cancer Working Group 2
97|criteria,21 with no secondary bone scan required to
98|confirm progression. Radiographic progression-free
99|survival was defined as the time between randomisation
100|and the occurrence of radiographical progression or
101|death from any cause. Overall survival was defined as the
102|time between randomisation and death from any cause.
103|Patients without events were censored at the date of last
104|follow-up.
105|The secondary endpoints were castration-resistant
106|prostate cancer (CRPC)-free survival, serious-genito
107|urinary-event-free survival, prostate-cancer-specific survival,
108|time to next skeletal-related event, PSA response rate,
109|prognostic study of serum PSA measured 6-8 months
110|after initiation of systemic therapy, time to pain pro
111|gression, time to chemotherapy for CRPC, quality of life,
112|changes in bone mineral density, correlation of biomarkers
113|with outcome, event rate per 100 person-years of treatment
114|analysis, and toxicity. CRPC-free survival was defined as

26|Statistical analysis
27|The initial protocol in 2013 planned for a sample size of
28|916 patients. However, due to a change in the SOC and the
29|knowledge gained from the LATITUDE and STAMPEDE
30|trial results published in late 2017, the planned sample
31|size was increased to 1173 and the coprimary study aims
32|were revised (appendix pp 7-8). Because PEACE-1 was the
33|only phase 3 trial to date that could determine abiraterone
34|efficacy in patients with mCSPC receiving ADT plus
35|docetaxel as SOC, the timing of the final analyses was
36|based on this population (population of interest). Sample
37|size calculation was performed with East software (Cytel;
38|Cambridge, MA, USA), on the basis of the assumption
39|that no significant interaction would take place between
40|radiotherapy and abiraterone, to allow for a 2 × 2 factorial
41|analysis of abiraterone efficacy. For abiraterone efficacy
42|evaluation, the predetermined acceptable probability of a
43|type I error was set at 0·05, divided between the two
44|coprimary endpoints (0·049 for overall survival and 0·001
45|for
46|radiographic
47|progression-free
48|survival).

50|hypothesised that adding abiraterone to ADT plus
51|docetaxel would improve overall survival by 30% over a
52|median of 53 months and progression-free survival by
53|40% over 30 months. Hence, with 355 patients assigned to
54|ADT with docetaxel plus abiraterone (with or without
55|radiotherapy) and 355 patients assigned to ADT with
56|docetaxel
57|without

59|(with
60|or

62|radiotherapy), 249 deaths would give an 80% power to
63|detect an overall survival hazard ratio (HR) of 0·70 at a
64|two-sided α level of 0·049. With the same group allocation,
65|262 radiographic progression events or deaths were
66|predicted to have an 80% power to detect a radiographic
67|progression-free survival HR of 0·60 at a two-sided α level
68|of 0·001.
69|This trial had a factorial design, based on the
70|assumption that there would be no interaction between
71|abiraterone and radiotherapy. Before analysing the
72|various outcomes, the presence of such an interaction
73|for both coprimary endpoints was tested by analyses of
74|maximum likelihood estimates using a Cox model
75|adjusted for stratification factors (ECOG performance
76|status [0 vs 1-2], ADT type [gonadotropin-releasing
77|hormone agonist vs antagonist vs bilateral orchiectomy],
78|metastatic burden [low vs high; as defined in the
79|Randomisation and masking section],2 and docetaxel
80|[no docetaxel before amendment vs no docetaxel after
81|amendment vs with docetaxel after amendment]). In the
82|absence of a qualitative interaction (p>0·05) between
83|abiraterone and radiotherapy, the groups were to be
84|combined two by two on the basis of abiraterone
85|administration, regardless of radiotherapy, before se
86|quentially assessing abiraterone efficacy first in the
87|overall population and then in the ADT with docetaxel
88|population (assuming the significance level was reached
89|in first instance). As the preplanned number of pro
90|gression-free survival and overall survival events had
91|not been reached in the study population at the time
92|this paper was written, the efficacy of radiotherapy
93|remains to be analysed (appendix p 16). The coprimary
94|endpoint results presented here correspond to the final
95|planned analysis; no interim analysis was conducted.
96|All efficacy analyses were conducted in the intention-to-
97|treat population, defined as all patients who were
98|randomly assigned to a treatment group. Safety analyses
99|were conducted in the safety population, according to
100|the treatment actually received by the patients (those
101|who did not receive any investigational treatment were
102|not included in the safety analyses).
103|The median follow-up was estimated by the inverse
104|Kaplan-Meier method. Time-to-event endpoints were
105|estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method. The Cox
106|proportional hazards model adjusted for radiotherapy
107|and stratification factors provided significances and an
108|estimate of the abiraterone effect (p value and HR with
109|CIs adjusted to match adjustment made to significance
110|levels in the corresponding test [ie, 99·9% for
111|radiographic progression-free survival, 95·1% for overall
112|survival, and 95% for secondary endpoints]). The
113|assumption of proportional hazards was evaluated on
114|the basis of the weighted Schoenfeld residuals. The
115|heterogeneity of the effect of abiraterone in the
116|predefined stratification subgroups was evaluated using
117|Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for radio
118|therapy and stratification factors and including an
119|interaction term between abiraterone and the studied
120|stratification variable. These analyses are illustrated
121|using forest plots. Notably, we analysed the efficacy of
122|abiraterone in the ADT with docetaxel population by
123|disease burden. Non-parametric CIs for the median
124|survival differences between groups were analysed by

4|Discussion
5|To our knowledge, this is the first trial to show that a
6|triple systemic therapy, consisting of ADT, docetaxel,
7|and a second-generation androgen signalling inhibitor
8|(abiraterone), extends radiographic progression-free survival
9|and overall survival in patients with de novo mCSPC.
10|Whether the systemic treatment of high-volume disease
11|(ie, extended metastatic spread) should differ from that of
12|low-volume disease has been extensively debated. The
13|benefit of ADT with docetaxel has been clearly shown for
14|patients with mCSPC with high-volume disease,4,22 but
15|data collected from larger populations support a similar
16|benefit across high-volume and low-volume disease.3 This
17|discrepancy might result from different ratios of patients
18|with de novo versus relapsing low-volume disease being
19|included in these trials, because recurrences favour better
20|prognoses.23 Second-generation androgen receptor axis
21|inhibitors have shown overall survival benefits in patients
22|with mCSPC regardless of the disease volume
23|considered.5,9,10 In this trial, the mature data for men with
24|high-volume disease indicate a clear improvement in
25|both radiographic progression-free survival and overall
26|survival when abiraterone is added to ADT with docetaxel.
27|Even though the data on overall survival were immature
28|for patients with low-volume disease, an abiraterone-
29|mediated benefit in radiographic progression-free
30|survival was already apparent. Thus, ADT with docetaxel
31|plus abiraterone should be proposed as a new SOC for
32|patients presenting with high-volume disease who are fit
33|for docetaxel prescription. However, for patients with low-
34|volume disease, the decision of whether to use two or
35|three agents should be carefully considered by both the
36|patients and their oncologists, to determine whether a
37|major benefit in radiographic progression-free survival
38|(HR 0·58) is sufficient to justify a treatment inten
39|sification in a context of immature overall survival data. It
40|would also depend on whether an overall survival benefit
41|is required. Long-term data and consensus conferences
42|will allow for clinical practice guidance refinement.
43|As abiraterone can inhibit CYP3A4 in vitro,24 and as
44|CYP3A4 is involved in docetaxel elimination,25 the
45|concomitant administration of these two drugs could
46|potentially increase docetaxel exposure and thereby its
47|toxicity. However, no increase in chemotherapy-related
48|side-effects occurred in reaction to this concomitance,
49|which might suggest an absence of substantial drug-
50|drug interactions between abiraterone and docetaxel.
51|This finding is consistent with the observation that
52|abiraterone and docetaxel have similar pharmacokinetic
53|behaviour when administered alone or in combination.26
54|Similarly, abiraterone did not affect the clearance of
55|another taxane, cabazitaxel, by CYP3A.27 We also did not
56|observe an increase in haematological toxicity when
57|abiraterone was added to ADT with docetaxel, contrary to
58|a phase 2 trial in patients with mCRPC.28 The most
59|frequent high-grade adverse event reported among
60|patients who received abiraterone in this trial was
61|hypertension (22% of patients who received abiraterone
62|vs 13% of those who did not). This expected adverse event

In addition, they do not display absolute cross- 7|resistance, as abiraterone improves overall survival 8|after docetaxel treatment and docetaxel retains some 9|activity after abiraterone failure.30,31 Collectively, these 10|observations provide a rationale for the survival benefits 11|resulting from their combination in this trial. However, 12|this study did not answer whether this triple 13|combination yields clinical advantages over ADT plus a 14|second-generation androgen receptor axis inhibitor. 15|Indeed, at the time when this trial was conducted 16|(2013-18), combining ADT with such an inhibitor had 17|not been approved for mCSPC, thereby precluding 18|such a comparison within the trial. Incidentally, the 19|ongoing phase 3 ARASENS (NCT02799602) and 20|ENZAMET (NCT02446405) trials are also testing the 21|combined efficacy of second-generation androgen 22|receptor axis inhibitors (darolutamide and enzalutamide, 23|respectively) with ADT and docetaxel, and their 24|upcoming overall survival results will put the benefits 25|of abiraterone in perspective. 26|Reaching treatment synergy and preventing acquired 27|resistance despite tumour clonal heterogeneity are 28|cardinal aspects of mCSPC management that require 29|an optimisation of the treatment framework. In 30|PEACE-1, significant survival benefits were obtained 31|when abiraterone was added to ADT with docetaxel. 32|Remarkably, these benefits were observed even though 33|more than 80% of the SOC without abiraterone group 34|eventually received a second-generation androgen 35|receptor axis inhibitor (mostly abiraterone or enzaluta 36|mide) to address cancer progression. Indeed, by contrast 37|with previous trials, PEACE-1 investigators were allowed 38|to prescribe early salvage treatments to the control 39|group patients who showed evidence of cancer 40|progression. To this end, a PSA minimum value of just 41|0·50 ng/mL was used to define mCRPC, even in the 42|absence of radiographic progression. Collectively, these 43|observations suggest that the upfront combination 44|implemented in this trial is superior to the sequential 45|administration of these (or similar) agents as occurred 46|in the control group. Of note, abiraterone is approved 47|for metastatic prostate cancer in many countries and is 48|close to becoming a worldwide generic drug. 49|In conclusion, this trial not only confirms that 50|combining abiraterone with SOC improves outcomes in 51|men with de novo mCSPC, but it shows that combining 52|abiraterone with ADT and docetaxel improves overall 53|and radiographic progression-free survival and other 54|efficacy 55|endpoints 56|with 57|little 58|toxicity 59|increase. 60|Nonetheless, as PEACE-1 only included patients with 61|de novo mCSPC, it is still unclear whether this triple 62|therapy might benefit patients with metachronous 63|mCSPC. Our findings cannot directly address whether 64|this triplet systemic combination is superior to ADT 65|and abiraterone. Longer follow-up is required to answer 66|whether combining such an intensive first line systemic 67|treatment with radiotherapy to the primary tumour 68|might provide further clinical benefits for patients with 69|mCSPC. # Assess deviations from intended interventions

Use this reference for Domain 2, which assesses the effect of assignment to
intervention. The returned question cards are authoritative.

For active conduct questions, build the chain in order:

1. What intervention was intended in each randomized group?
2. What change, non-adherence, or additional intervention occurred?
3. Did the trial context cause that change?
4. Could it affect the outcome, and was it balanced between groups?

For 2.3, a negative answer covers no relevant deviation as well as changes that
were protocol-consistent or could occur outside the trial context. An affirmative
answer needs evidence or strong reason linking a protocol-inconsistent deviation
to the trial context. State that link when it is an inference.
A protocol establishes the plan, not conduct. Different assigned treatments or
visible schedules do not by themselves prove that participants or carers knew
the assignment.

For 2.6, assess the analysis separately. Compare randomized assignment with the analyzed
population, exclusions, reassignment, and reasons. An ITT label is not proof
that all randomized participants were analyzed as assigned. Excluding only
participants with missing outcome data is not automatically the same as an
inappropriate assignment-effect analysis; keep that issue distinct for Domain
3. If an analysis defect activates the impact question, consider outcome rarity
and prognostic exclusions as well as the percentage affected.

Support each conduct-chain proposition with source facts and any stated
inference. A passage supporting one proposition does not settle the others.

# Assess missing outcome data

Use this reference for Domain 3. The approved Result fixes the outcome and time
point; the returned question cards fix answer direction and activation.

Every active answer is accompanied by a concise justification, an `unknowns`
array (use `[]` when none are identified), and a `counterevidence` array. A
counterpoint refers to the answer's zero-based basis index, for example:

```json
"counterevidence": [{"basis_index": 0, "implication": "This passage limits the strength of the selected answer."}]
```

Inactive branch answers may be omitted or retained without fabricated reasoning;
the server commits only the dependency-closed active path.

## Availability audit

For D3.1, support Yes or Probably Yes with actual outcome-availability
evidence. Accept one or more of:

- comparable observed-outcome counts for the randomized population;
- arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring rates, reasons, and follow-up
  accounting; or
- an explicit statement that ascertainment was complete or nearly complete.

The following do not establish affirmative availability on their own:

- analysis denominators or ITT membership;
- planned or scheduled follow-up;
- treatment continuation or discontinuation; or
- a generic censoring rule without actual rates or follow-up accounting.

For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later
time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not
establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect
outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their
outcome and time window to the approved Result. Recovery may inform bias from
missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

When the availability premise remains unresolved, use the active comparison
card's full Source inventory to inspect unopened supplements or combined
protocol documents. Search for concrete study wording such as the outcome
status, withdrawal or loss-to-follow-up labels, and the reported time point;
`missing outcome data` alone may not occur in the report. Widen the Source
scope or continue a cached cursor only as needed, and stop when comparable
observed counts or complete follow-up accounting are inspected. If the
captured Sources and bounded page windows do not establish availability,
document that limit instead of treating an empty Source group or a no-hit
search as evidence of missing outcomes.

## Reconcile availability

Keep these quantities distinct for each arm and time point:

- randomized participants;
- participants with the outcome observed;
- participants included in the reported analysis;
- participants whose outcomes were imputed; and
- post-randomization exclusions.

An analyzed count is not necessarily an observed count. Imputed outcomes count
as missing outcome data for RoB 2. Treatment discontinuation is not missing
outcome data when follow-up and outcome ascertainment continued.

If some outcomes are missing, assess whether data remain available for nearly
all randomized participants. Consider whether the missing outcomes could make
an important difference to this Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare the
missing count with observed events, not only the randomized denominator.
A count below the randomized total does not settle that question.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring
caused by missing follow-up before the outcome could be observed. For time-to-event Results,
censoring may still create missing outcome information; assess its timing,
reason, and relation to treatment or prognosis instead of treating every
censored participant as either fully observed or missing by default.

When a count comparison would help before answering, call `get_domain_context`
with `missing_data` rows. Every preview row needs a nonempty `basis` containing
current-Trial Evidence references: no answer exists to supply inherited Evidence.
Inspect `comparison_cards[].missing_data`
for differences, fractions, and conflicting reports. The preview changes no
checkpoint or State revision. To retain the chosen rows, submit them with the
3.1 answer in `validate_domain_assessment`; omit row `basis` there only to reuse
the answer's Evidence when it supports those counts. After its receipt, save
the exact draft with `save_domain_judgment`.

Check each input against its source passage before using the arithmetic. The
helper subtracts supplied observed counts from randomized counts; it does not
extract counts or sum grouped departures. Keep unknown observed counts unknown.
Skip the preview when an explicit ascertainment statement resolves availability
without arithmetic.

## Assess bias from missingness

If data were not available for all or nearly all participants, ask in sequence:

1. Does a bias-correcting method or informative sensitivity analysis show that
   the Result was not biased?
2. Could missingness depend on the true outcome, based on reasons, health
   status, withdrawal, loss to follow-up, or censoring?
3. If it could, is that dependence likely given arm differences, reasons,
   prognostic factors, or trial circumstances?

Simple imputation, including last observation carried forward or multiple
imputation based only on intervention group, does not by itself show freedom from
bias. Documented reasons support reassurance only when they address the outcome
relationship.

Keep possible dependence in 3.3 separate from likely dependence in 3.4. For
3.4, state which reasons or trial circumstances support the likelihood judgment.
Absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likely dependence. Preserve
`no_information` when the card's uncertainty rule applies, even when that answer
leads to High risk of bias.

D3.2 does not allow `no_information`. When no bias-correcting evidence is found,
use the question card to choose a permitted negative or probably-negative answer
with the appropriate limitation or Evidence basis. Do not fabricate direct
support for the absence of bias.

# Assess outcome measurement

Use this reference for Domain 4. The approved Result fixes the outcome; the
returned question cards are authoritative. Apply this ordered audit:

1. Start from the approved Result's event definition and ascertainment method.
2. Assess whether the measurement method is appropriate for that approved event.
3. Compare methods, thresholds, schedules, and detection opportunities between
   randomized groups.
4. Identify who determines whether that event occurred, not merely who records
   it. For participant-reported outcomes, the participant is the assessor.
5. Answer assessor awareness separately from susceptibility to influence.
6. If influence is possible or likely, explain the mechanism. Assess possibility
   before likelihood. If no mechanism can be established, apply the official
   uncertainty guidance.
7. For all-cause mortality, distinguish establishing death from judging
   progression, symptoms, or cause of death.
8. For composite outcomes, consider every component that can determine the event.
9. When a passage discusses several outcomes, use only the premise that applies
   to the approved outcome and state any inference or unresolved link.

An endpoint label does not prove validity or objectivity. A shared time origin,
analysis population, or planned protocol does not prove equal actual assessment.
An open-label design alone does not decide method suitability, differential
measurement, or likely influence. Additional visits, passive detection, or
different thresholds matter only through their effect on outcome ascertainment.

# Assess selection of the reported result

Use this reference for Domain 5. The approved Result is fixed; do not switch to
an easier endpoint. The returned question cards are authoritative.

## Establish the analysis plan

Identify the exact planned outcome measurement, definition, time point,
population, analysis, and effect estimate. Establish that the plan was finalized
before unblinded outcome data were available, or that later changes were
unrelated to the results. Then compare the plan with the approved reported
Result.

Use captured Source provenance to locate the applicable plan passages. The
active comparison card lists every captured Source, including supplements and
combined protocol documents with no selected passages. Compare
their version, date, intervention groups, and cohort with the approved Result.
In `comparison_cards[].passage_groups`, inspect the Source label, role, logical
path, page count, and content and projection hashes. A protocol, SAP, or registry
group may have no selected passages yet. Use the Source to resolve missing
premises; an empty passage list does not establish absent plan content.
`source_origin`, `registry_url`, and `registry_retrieved_at` describe captured
provenance; they do not establish when a plan was finalized or which Trial
comparison it covered.

For a registry group with `registry_recovery`, call `read_pages` with that
object's `trial_id` and `windows`. Inspect the captured fields identified by
`registry_field_paths`. These are navigation paths into the immutable projection,
not a historical plan or an applicability judgment. `windows` contains at most
20 windows; `registry_window_count` reports the total. If more remain, navigate
the captured Source using its page count and `search_sources` with the field
paths. Refreshing context does not advance these registry windows. For omitted selected
passages, follow [Recover omitted Evidence](evidence.md#recover-omitted-evidence).

Keep record posting, record update, retrieval, plan finalization, recruitment,
and unblinded access dates distinct. A registry's first-posted date does not
date the endpoint content in its current record.

The selected plan passage establishes plan content. A registry identifier,
endpoint label, or report-level prespecification claim alone leaves plan timing
and correspondence unresolved. A probable answer still needs a stated basis for
the timing judgment; the report's "a priori" label alone does not supply it.
For a platform trial, establish that the plan applies to the approved intervention
comparison and cohort. A protocol or SAP
describes intent; check the report for what was actually done.

If the plan is unavailable after bounded source-specific discovery, record that
information limit. Missing plans do not prove selective reporting.
Keep unknown dates and historical applicability explicit. Use captured versions
and exact recovery windows. Use only captured Sources for this assessment. A
current record cannot stand in for an unseen past version.

For an unresolved plan premise, search with concrete wording from the report or
plan (for example, the endpoint label, analysis population, time point, or
section heading). Continue an existing cursor when deeper cached results may
contain the plan. Issue another bounded query or widen the Source scope only
when it could resolve the premise. Read the complete returned window, including
its date and cohort context, before treating it as a plan passage. Stop on a
complete applicable comparison or document the bounded information limit with
an explicit stopping rationale and, when useful, the current search receipt. A
Source role or an empty passage list cannot establish either plan presence or
plan absence.

## Separate the two selection mechanisms

For eligible outcome measurements, compare alternative scales, definitions,
thresholds, time points, or assessors. Ask whether only a subset was fully
reported and whether selection was likely based on the results.

For eligible analyses, compare alternative adjustment sets, transformations,
models, composite definitions, censoring rules, missing-data methods,
populations, or effect estimates. Apply the same selection question separately.

For 5.3, identify both the eligible alternatives and evidence that reporting
favoured a subset because of its results. Reporting ITT, per-protocol, imputed,
and survival analyses together establishes multiplicity, not that selection
occurred. An inability to rule out selection does not support Yes/Probably Yes.
When intentions are insufficiently detailed and multiple analyses were possible,
use No information unless other evidence resolves the selection question.

A detailed reported endpoint or estimate proves neither prespecification nor the
absence of alternatives. For a non-exact Result, compare the exact approved
definition and relation rationale with the plan; do not silently assess a more
convenient planned endpoint.

evidence_needed: Outcome type, assessor role, degree of judgement, and whether knowledge of assignment could change assessment.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when possible influence cannot be determined; this question is conditional on awareness in 4.3.

questions.decision_rule: Distinguish possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from likely influence. Strong beliefs about benefits or harms make influence more likely, for example patient-reported symptoms in homeopathy or recovery assessed by an intervention physiotherapist.

Knowledge could have influenced assessment but it was not likely to do so.

considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

Likely influence requires more than assessor awareness or a possible pathway: look for evidence it occurred, or strong beliefs and a real judgement opportunity. Keep this conclusion separate from measurement susceptibility and detection opportunity.
